lessons.title: Greeting coworkers
lessons.objective: Greet a peer or a client correctly for the time of day and answer '¿Cómo está?'
lessons.hook: Your first words each day set the tone with your Peruvian team.
lessons.explain: Hola means hello and works at any time of day. For a time-specific greeting, buenos días is used in the morning, buenas tardes in the afternoon, buenas noches in the evening or at night. ¿Cómo estás? asks 'how are you?' to a friend or peer. ¿Cómo está? (usted) is the polite form for a boss, client, or elder. Bien, gracias means 'fine, thanks'. Example: at 9 a.m. you meet your client: 'Buenos días, señor Ramos. ¿Cómo está?' He replies: 'Bien, gracias.'
key_facts: Hola means hello and works at any time of day.
Buenos días is used in the morning, buenas tardes in the afternoon, buenas noches in the evening or at night.
¿Cómo estás? asks 'how are you?' to a friend or peer.
¿Cómo está? (usted) is the polite form for a boss, client, or elder.
Bien, gracias means 'fine, thanks'.
angles: Think of two dials: the time of day picks días/tardes/noches, and the person picks estás (peer) or está (client).
Hola is your safe all-day word; add buenos días or buenas tardes to sound more professional.

Buenas tardes is an afternoon greeting.

lessons.title: Writing Spanish: ¿ ¡ ñ and capitals
lessons.objective: Write short Spanish sentences with correct opening marks, ñ, accents and capitalization
lessons.hook: Your coworkers will read your chat messages; correct marks make you look careful.
lessons.aside: Spanish t and d are dental, made with the tongue against the upper teeth, much like Hindi त and द, not like English t and d.
lessons.explain: Spanish questions open with ¿ and close with ?: ¿Cómo estás? Exclamations open with ¡ and close with !: ¡Hola! The letter ñ is a separate letter, sounding like 'ny' in 'canyon'. After a comma, a word is not capitalized unless it is a name. Accent marks can change meaning: tú (you) vs tu (your). Example of a chat message: 'Hola, Ana. ¿Cómo estás? ¡Gracias por tu ayuda!' Here 'Hola, Ana' keeps Ana capital because it is a name, while a normal word after a comma stays lowercase.

Exclamations open with ¡ and close with !.
ñ is a separate letter, sounding like 'ny' in 'canyon'.

fixes: Capitalizing an ordinary word right after a comma, as in 'Mi llamo Alex, Mi work'.

lessons.title: Saying your name: Me llamo
lessons.objective: Introduce yourself, ask someone's name and respond politely
lessons.hook: Introducing yourself is the first thing you will do with every new Peruvian coworker.
lessons.explain: Me llamo ___ means 'My name is ___' (literally 'I call myself'). Me means 'myself'; mi means 'my'. So 'Mi llamo' is wrong; say 'Me llamo'. To ask back, ¿Cómo te llamas? asks a peer's name; ¿Cómo se llama? asks politely. Mucho gusto means 'nice to meet you'. Example: 'Hola, me llamo Alex. ¿Cómo se llama?' — 'Me llamo Lucía. Mucho gusto.' — 'Mucho gusto.'

lessons.title: Tú or usted: choosing 'you'
lessons.objective: Choose tú, usted or ustedes correctly for people at work
lessons.hook: Using the right 'you' with a Peruvian client shows respect.
lessons.explain: Tú is informal 'you' for friends and peers. Usted is formal 'you' for clients, bosses and elders. Usted takes the same verb form as él/ella (he/she): usted está, like ella está. Ustedes is plural 'you' in Peru and all of Latin America, for both formal and informal. In a new workplace, start with usted until someone uses tú with you. Example: to the client, '¿Usted está en Lima?'; to the team, '¿Ustedes están listos?'; later, a friendly coworker says '¿Tú estás bien?' and you can use tú back.
key_facts: Tú is informal 'you' for friends and peers.
Usted is formal 'you' for clients, bosses and elders.
Usted takes the same verb form as él/ella (he/she): usted está.
Ustedes is plural 'you' in Peru and all of Latin America, for both formal and informal.
In a new workplace, start with usted until someone uses tú with you.

Usted grammatically behaves like 'he/she', so ella está and usted está share the same verb.

lessons.title: Estar: I am (feeling / located)
lessons.objective: Conjugate estar in the present and say how and where you are
lessons.hook: 'Estoy bien' and 'Estoy en la oficina' are sentences you will use daily.
lessons.explain: Estar means 'to be' for states and location. Present forms: yo estoy, tú estás, usted/él/ella está, nosotros estamos, ustedes/ellos están. 'Estu' is not a Spanish word; 'I am' with estar is 'estoy'. Estoy bien means 'I am fine'. Estoy en la oficina means 'I am in the office'. Example: a coworker writes '¿Cómo estás? ¿Dónde estás?' You reply: 'Estoy bien. Estoy en la oficina.' Notice the ¿Cómo estás? you already know is just estar with tú.

lessons.title: Ser: I am (who / from where / what job)
lessons.objective: Use ser to state identity, origin and profession, and choose it over estar
lessons.hook: Telling coworkers where you're from and what you do needs ser.
lessons.explain: Ser means 'to be' for identity, origin and profession. Present: yo soy, tú eres, usted/él/ella es, nosotros somos, ustedes/ellos son. Spanish drops 'a/an' before a profession after ser: Soy ingeniero, not 'Soy un ingeniero'. Soy de ___ means 'I am from ___'. Use estar, not ser, for how you feel right now. Example: 'Soy Alex. Soy de la India. Soy ingeniero. Hoy estoy bien.' Likewise, 'my job is interesting' is 'Mi trabajo es interesante', with ser, because it describes what the job is like.

lessons.title: Hoy, mañana, ayer
lessons.objective: Talk about today, tomorrow, yesterday and the morning without confusing them
lessons.hook: Mixing up 'today' and 'tomorrow' can make you miss a deadline.
lessons.explain: Hoy means 'today'. Mañana means 'tomorrow'. With la, la mañana means 'the morning'. Ayer means 'yesterday'. Mañana por la mañana means 'tomorrow morning'. Without ñ, 'manana' is a misspelling; ñ is needed. Example: a coworker writes 'La reunión es mañana por la mañana, no hoy.' That means the meeting is tomorrow morning, not today. If you read 'mañana' as today, you would show up a day early.
